Alternatively, use Meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours, Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Amikacin 15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours. 3. Another option is Imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours or 1 g every 8 hours, combined with Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours. 4. Alternatively, use Imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours or 1 g every 8 hours, Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Tobramycin 5–7 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours. 5. Another regimen includes Imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours or 1 g every 8 hours, Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Amikacin 15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours. 6. Doripenem 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours, Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours is another preferred regimen. 7. Alternatively, administer Doripenem 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours, Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Tobramycin 5–7 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours. 8. Another option is Doripenem 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours, Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours, and Amikacin 15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 24 hours. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA): The preferred regimen is Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours. Note: Antimicrobial therapy for established infections should generally be limited to 4–7 days unless achieving adequate source control is challenging. Prolonged therapy durations have not been associated with improved outcomes. For esophagitis caused by Candida: The preferred regimen is Fluconazole 100–200 mg daily orally or intravenously for 14–21 days. Alternative regimens include: 1. Itraconazole suspension 100–200 mg orally twice daily. 2. Voriconazole 200 mg orally twice daily. 3. Amphotericin B 0.3–0.7 mg/kg/day intravenously for 7 days. 4. Caspofungin 50 mg/day intravenously following a 70 mg loading dose. 5. Micafungin 150 mg/day intravenously. 6. Anidulafungin 50 mg/day intravenously following a 100 mg loading dose. Note: Maintenance therapy with Fluconazole 100–200 mg/day orally is recommended for AIDS patients. For esophagitis caused by herpes simplex virus: Preferred regimens include: 1. Acyclovir 5 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours for 7–14 days. 2. Acyclovir 400 mg orally five times daily for 14–21 days. 3. Valacyclovir 1 g orally three times daily for 14–21 days, with or without maintenance suppressive therapy in AIDS patients. Alternative regimens include: 1. Famciclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 14–21 days. 2. Foscarnet 90 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours for 7–14 days. For cytomegalovirus (CMV): The preferred regimen is Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–21 days. Alternative regimens include: 1. Foscarnet 90 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours for 14–21 days, followed by 90–120 mg/kg/day intravenously for maintenance in AIDS patients. 2. Valganciclovir 900 mg orally twice daily, then 900 mg orally once daily for maintenance in AIDS patients. Note: Maintenance therapy with Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg/day intravenously or 6 mg/kg/day intravenously for 5 days per week is recommended for AIDS patients. For aphthous ulceration in immunocompromised hosts: The preferred regimen is Prednisone 40 mg/day orally for 14 days, tapered over 4–8 weeks. An alternative regimen is Thalidomide 200 mg/day orally. For hepatic abscess: Pending determination of bacterial versus amoebic liver abscess: 1. Preferred regimen: Metronidazole 30–40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses intravenously every 8 hours or 500 mg orally every 6–8 hours, combined with Ceftriaxone 1–2 g intravenously every 24 hours or Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g intravenously every 4–6 hours. 2. Another preferred regimen: Metronidazole 30–40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses intravenously every 8 hours or 500 mg orally every 6–8 hours, combined with Ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours or 750 mg orally, or Levofloxacin 750 mg orally/intravenously every 24 hours. 3. Alternative regimen: Metronidazole 30–40 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses intravenously every 8 hours or 500 mg orally every 6–8 hours, combined with Ertapenem 1 g intravenously every 24 hours. For hepatitis A: Supportive care is usually sufficient, with no restrictions on diet or activity. For acute hepatitis B: No specific therapy is available; treatment is supportive. Prevention: Vaccination remains the best strategy, especially in high-risk groups. Universal vaccination is recommended in countries with high prevalence. For chronic hepatitis B: Patients with HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B: 1. If HBV DNA > 20,000 IU/mL and ALT < 2 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), observe and consider treatment when ALT becomes elevated. 2. Consider biopsy in individuals > 40 years old, with persistently high-normal ALT > 2 times ULN, or with a family history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 3. Initiate treatment if HBV DNA > 20,000 IU/mL and biopsy shows moderate/severe inflammation or significant fibrosis. If HBV DNA > 20,000 IU/mL and ALT > 2 times ULN: 1. Preferred regimen: Pegylated IFN-alpha 180 mcg weekly subcutaneously for 48 weeks. 2. Preferred regimen: Tenofovir (TDF) with dosage adjustments based on creatinine clearance. 3. Preferred regimen: Entecavir (ETV) with dosage adjustments based on creatinine clearance. Treatment duration is a minimum of 1 year, continuing for at least 6 months after HBeAg seroconversion.
